Before becoming guides at the local history room, we had a week of (1) training. We learnt where visitors could stand and which objects must not be touched. During the final practice, our teacher (2) hid a small wooden spoon under a cloth and asked us to describe it without seeing it.

The spoon was the (3) oldest object in the display. The dates on the labels showed that every other item had been made more recently. We had to come to a (4) decision about the best way to introduce it. A long list of dates did not seem helpful for young visitors.

One child asked us (5) when the people who had used the spoon would return. It was a surprising question, but it reminded us that the dates needed explaining. We found it (6) useful to connect the spoon with objects the child could recognise from home.

The narrow space near the door also needed attention. Visitors had to move through it (7) safely, particularly when another group was coming in. On our (8) second day as guides, we moved one chair so that the doorway was clear. We had noticed the problem on the first day, but had needed permission before changing anything.

By the end of the week, several (9) visitors had left short messages thanking the school. The history room's coordinator said the improvement was (10) ours, not just the teacher's. I was pleased, though I also knew how much help we had received before feeling confident enough to speak.
